reply.summary: Mechanism diagram: non-reference template (identity and RNA yield unknown) -> putative RNA species X -> preferential adsorption at the P-V internal boundary -> reduced effective interfacial free-energy cost -> conditional cavity persistence. Here P is the surrounding RNA-rich phase and V the RNA-poor cavity phase; X is a proposed interfacial layer, not a measured third bulk phase. For a macroscopic X layer between P and V, S_X = gamma_PV - gamma_PX - gamma_XV; S_X >= 0 is the complete-wetting criterion under this three-interface convention. Each gamma and S_X has units of energy/area. The relation is conditional physical reasoning, not evidence that wetting occurs here. The measured observable prediction is a calibrated, sequence-specific boundary/adjacent-dense X signal ratio greater than 1 among cavity-bearing droplets, associated with persistence after conditioning on local bulk signal. Bulk demixing does not require selective boundary enrichment, though incidental enrichment is possible. Smallest discriminating measurement: establish the transcribed X identity, then quantify its signal per calibrated area at cavity boundaries versus immediately adjacent dense phase in the same droplets while tracking cavity persistence. E01 reports only a population mean area fraction; E02 associates template fractions with a distinct endpoint; E03 lacks cavity-state trajectories; E04 measures bulk tie-line endpoints without mapping them to cavity interiors; E05 DNA read fractions do not determine RNA abundance. The returned S1 abstract supports only the broad relevance of coupled associative and segregative transitions in multivalent proteins/nucleic acids; it says nothing about internal RNA interfaces, selective wetting, or the proposed enrichment test. S2 is a broad crowding review and offers no direct support for this mechanism.

sources.title: Phase Transitions of Associative Biomacromolecules.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Multivalent proteins and nucleic acids, collectively referred to as multivalent associative biomacromolecules, provide the driving forces for the formation and compositional regulation of biomolecular condensates. Here, we review the key concepts of phase transitions of aqueous solutions of associative biomacromolecules, specifically proteins that include folded domains and intrinsically disordered regions. The phase transitions of these systems come under the rubric of coupled associative and segregative transitions. The concepts underlying these processes are presented, and their relevance to biomolecular condensates is discussed.

sources.title: Molecular Crowding: The History and Development of a Scientific Paradigm.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: It is now generally accepted that macromolecules do not act in isolation but "live" in a crowded environment, that is, an environment populated by numerous different molecules. The field of molecular crowding has its origins in the far 80s but became accepted only by the end of the 90s. In the present issue, we discuss various aspects that are influenced by crowding and need to consider its effects. This Review is meant as an introduction to the theme and an analysis of the evolution of the crowding concept through time from colloidal and polymer physics to a more biological perspective. We introduce themes that will be more thoroughly treated in other Reviews of the present issue. In our intentions, each Review may stand by itself, but the complete collection has the aspiration to provide different but complementary perspectives to propose a more holistic view of molecular crowding.
